pillars.title: Keep the core value free, don't take it away with an update
pillars.dek: People don't leave over price, they leave because the feature they came for and spent years filling up suddenly got hidden behind a subscription. The right mechanic is to charge for what's new, not to take away what's familiar.

pillars.title: Match what the person sees on the water
pillars.dek: The bite forecast, the depth, the tide and the wind get checked literally, the angler drives to the water and compares. A single mismatch zeroes out trust in the whole app, so the number has to line up with reality rather than just look nice.

pillars.title: Cover the water exactly where the person fishes
pillars.dek: Maps, spots and reports are dead if your lake, river or state isn't in them and nobody nearby has posted. The value isn't in the size of the database overall, it's in the density of data under the user's specific water.

couples-relationship.governing: The couples-app niche splits not by price and not by feature count, but by the specific job a couple hires the product to do every day. The first and densest cluster of demand is the daily ritual of getting to know each other again through questions, quizzes and games. This is where Paired, Evergreen, Lasting, Cozy Couples, Lovewick, SumOne, Candle, Coral and Couples land. Here couples aren't looking for anyone new, they're trying to start talking again, and the product lasts exactly until the day the questions run out or start repeating. That's precisely where the leaders break. On Evergreen and Coral people burn through the whole question bank in a couple of months and write that no new content shows up, on Lovewick dozens of reviews say there used to be ten cards a day and now there's one, on Couples people complain there have been no new questions for half a year. The second cluster is the shared connective layer between two phones: a day counter, a home-screen widget, notes and drawings, a private chat. This is home to My Love, Between, noteit, Just Between Us, Couple Widget, LiveStatus, Couple360 and The Couple. The job is simple but the stakes are high, because people keep years of shared photos and messages in it. When Between loses five years of pictures or Couple Widget's widget image breaks, the couple leaves for good and furious. The widget here isn't decoration but the only reason to come back, and the moment it goes blank or sync stalls, the app is forgotten. The third cluster is a shared living object and a structured path: a pet or a tree the couple grows together (Widgetable, Love8, Couple Tree, Cozy Couples), a love-tank level (Love Nudge) and real therapy with lessons and sessions (Lasting, ReGain, Relatio). The strengths are where the couple gets a shared object of care or a step-by-step program, and the failures are where the living object turns into feeding for coins (Widgetable, Love8) or where the program cuts off with no feedback (Lasting, ReGain). One fault line runs through the whole niche. The product only works when both partners are in it, and any imbalance, when one partner doesn't answer, when the two answers don't match, when the second account breaks, ruins the whole point, because unlike an ordinary app you can't use this one alone.
couples-relationship.competitorRead: The players break into several types. The indie small fry with a one-time or cheap payment, that's My Love, Couple Widget, The Couple, noteit, Couple Tree, wins on simplicity and instant usefulness: set a date, pin a widget, send a drawing. But it sags on reliability, because dates drift, widgets go blank, history is lost and support stays silent. The subscription mainstreams of questions and analysis, that's Paired, Evergreen, Lasting, Cozy Couples, Lovewick, are strong on thoughtful content and genuinely bring people closer, but all of them hit one wall: the question bank is finite, and within a month or two the couple has nothing left to open, while the old free content slides behind a paywall on top of that, leaving loyal users feeling cheated. The hybrids with a pet and currency, that's Widgetable, Love8, SumOne, LiveStatus, hook people with cuteness and shared care, but break their own idea when caring for the pet turns into endless feeding for coins and ads, and on LiveStatus the pets and statuses themselves fail to load for years. Standing apart are the deep-work products: ReGain with live therapists, Lasting and Relatio with lessons. Here people value the specialists and the content, but the tech, the partner pairing and a program that cuts off mid-way all keep the couple from reaching a result. Private messengers for two, that's Between and Just Between Us, win by replacing the couple's ordinary chat and keeping the intimate stuff separate, and lose in exactly the same place: when encryption breaks or photos won't load, they lose the only thing they were kept for.

pillars.title: The daily ritual holds the couple together until the content runs out
pillars.dek: The main engine of the niche is the daily question or card that gets the couple talking again. It works flawlessly as long as there's something to open, and dies the day the question bank repeats or runs dry.

pillars.title: The shared layer between two phones: the connection is worth exactly as much as it is reliable
pillars.dek: A widget, a day counter, notes and a private chat keep the couple in touch every day, and years of shared history pile up inside them. Any sync failure, blank widget or lost photo ruins the only reason to come back.

pillars.title: A couple hires the product only as two, and any imbalance breaks everything
pillars.dek: A couples app can't be used alone, so the product rests on both partners showing up together. When one partner cools off, the two answers don't match or the second account breaks, the whole point is lost for both at once.

hiking-trails.governing: The hiking-app market is built around one job people hire an app to do out in the woods with no signal: keep me from getting lost. Everything else, finding trails, planning, pretty videos, is secondary, and that is exactly where the market splits into several different demands and the leaders break on the one thing that matters most. The first and deepest split is offline navigation. People pay for a subscription precisely to get a downloaded map, and out on the trail with no signal they get nothing. AllTrails with a paid Plus membership hands back a downloaded map that reads Not available in the middle of a hike, FarOut simply stops opening after three days on a thru-hike, OnX endlessly calculates the download size and never downloads, Gaia won't pin the track to the trail offline, and OS Maps logs you out when their server goes down, and then even the downloaded maps are unreachable. Against that backdrop the tiny Tomstrails wins by honestly working on GPS alone in airplane mode and saving battery, and Topo Map & Hiking Tracker gets praised for offline and airplane mode. The second cluster is route planning that actually follows the trails. Footpath draws a straight line instead of the trail's curve and refuses to use footpaths, Gaia's trail snapping falls off half the time, OnX drops random points on its own and won't let you remove them, komoot took away the ability to reorder points. The third cluster is fresh on-trail conditions from other people. That is why people keep WTA (trip reports are the entire point of the app) and FarOut (water, bear and hostel markers, a game changer), but FarOut launched an AI that deleted years of useful comments, and AllTrails draws complaints about AI slop in its descriptions. Standing apart are the smaller, precise jobs: effort tracking (Topo Map consistently logs 18 miles instead of 14 and won't count the second climb, Walkmeter dies mid-walk, Wikiloc records triple the distance) and safety (the whole point of Cairn, family sees your location and coverage zone, but it stops recording the track right on the route). The leaders all break along one common line: with every update a favorite feature is removed and hidden behind the subscription (Avenza killed importing your own maps, Relive removed track trimming, Gaia dropped the Nat Geo layers), and the interface is redone so that finding a trail gets harder.
hiking-trails.competitorRead: Three different types of players live in this niche. Indies with a one-time purchase win on honesty and on staying out of the way: Tomstrails gets praised outright for hiding nothing behind a subscription and pushing no ads, Topo Map & Hiking Tracker is loved for no subscription, no ads and for owning rather than renting, WorkOutDoors buys the same loyalty from former Garmin owners. Their weak spot is narrowness and small holes: Tomstrails has no coordinate formats, Topo Map is forever wrong on mileage, WorkOutDoors has an interface you drown in without documentation. The subscription mainstreams, AllTrails, Gaia, onX, komoot, Wikiloc, Outdooractive, hold share through the sheer size of their trail base and their maps, but they lose people the same way: constant pop-ups pitching a subscription on every tap, offline that lets you down, and redesigns that break the familiar flow. A separate painful subgroup is the acquired projects: OnX bought Hiking Project and the REI projects and turned them into nagware wrappers, Outdooractive killed the beloved ViewRanger, Bending Spoons rewrote komoot, Outside bought Gaia and pulled the layers. People say outright that they leave for alternatives after this. Finally the nonprofit and niche ones, WTA, Outdoor Afro, OuterSpatial, National Park Trail Guide, are strong on content and community (nothing else compares to WTA's reports), but they fall down on the tech: WTA has crashed on search and failed to load the map for years, National Park Trail Guide just stops opening after an update.

pillars.title: make a downloaded map that honestly works with no signal
pillars.dek: This is the niche's biggest unfilled job. People pay precisely for the offline map, and out on the trail with no signal the leaders hand back nothing or crash. Whoever nails offline so it can be trusted as the single source of navigation takes a market the giants exited in words only.

pillars.title: let people build a route that follows the real trails
pillars.dek: Planning breaks when the line won't pin to the trail: it draws straight instead of curving, points can't be removed or reordered, the route steers onto roads. A tool where the track obediently snaps to the actual trail and is easy to edit right with a finger removes a pain the mass-market apps solve only halfway.

pillars.title: show fresh on-trail conditions from people who walked it recently
pillars.dek: For the sake of recent reports and markers (water, deadfall, snow, bears, trail condition) people keep an app and fill it themselves. Whoever builds a stream of fresh, verifiable posts from people who just walked it and doesn't wipe them with an AI purge closes the job people pay for with attention and money.
